cards.front: What should you know about cells are the basic building blocks of all living organisms.?
cards.back: In multicellular organisms, cells become specialised for particular functions. Similar cells group together to form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in organ systems.

cards.front: What should you know about multicellular organisms?
cards.back: are organised into a hierarchy: cells specialise, group into tissues, tissues combine into organs, and organs form organ systems. This allows large organisms to function efficiently.

cards.front: What should you know about animal tissues?
cards.back: include muscular tissue (for movement), glandular tissue (for producing secretions), and epithelial tissue (for covering surfaces). Each tissue is made of cells specialised for its function.

cards.front: Recall a key point about B4 Tissues And Organs
cards.back: These three tissues are found in the stomach. Muscular tissue churns food, glandular tissue produces digestive juices, and epithelial tissue lines the inside surface.

cards.front: What should you know about plant tissues?
cards.back: include epidermal tissue (covering), palisade mesophyll (photosynthesis), spongy mesophyll (gas exchange), xylem (water transport) and phloem (sugar transport).

cards.front: What should you know about the stomach?
cards.back: is an example of an organ made of multiple tissues working together. It contains muscular tissue, glandular tissue and epithelial tissue, each performing a different role in digestion.

cards.front: What should you know about key principle?
cards.back: An organ contains different tissues because it needs to perform several functions. Each tissue is specialised for one of those functions.

cards.front: What should you know about the digestive system?
cards.back: is an organ system made of several organs working together to break down large food molecules into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.

cards.front: Recall a key point about B4 Tissues And Organs
cards.back: Mathematical skills in this topic are minimal. Focus on interpreting diagrams and understanding hierarchical organisation. You may need to calculate the surface area to volume ratio of exchange surfaces (e.g. villi) to explain why larger surface area increases absorption.

cards.front: What should you know about answer?
cards.back: Individual palisade cells (cell level) group into palisade mesophyll tissue (tissue level). Multiple tissues including palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, epidermal tissue, xylem and phloem combine to form the leaf (organ level). The leaf works with roots and stems in the plant transport and photosynthetic systems (organ system level).
The basic unit of life, specialised for a function (e.g. Muscle cell, nerve cell, sperm cell)
A group of similar cells with the same function (e.g. Muscular tissue, epithelial tissue)
A group of tissues working together (e.g. Stomach, heart, leaf)
A group of organs working together (e.g. Digestive system, circulatory system)
A living individual made of organ systems (e.g. Human, oak tree)
